notes.meaning: Jesus questioned Judas for using a kiss, which was a normal greeting of love and respect between a rabbi and his student, as a sign to betray Him. By calling Himself the 'Son of Man,' Jesus reminded Judas of His role as the promised Messiah and King. He showed that He was fully aware of the false friendship and treachery taking place.

When the disciples saw that the armed crowd was about to seize Jesus, they asked if they should fight with their swords. They had two swords with them and wanted to protect their Master. Their desire to defend Him was sincere, but they did not yet understand that God's plan was for Jesus to submit willingly.

Before waiting for Jesus to reply, one disciple swung his sword and cut off the right ear of the high priest's servant. Luke, who was a medical doctor, carefully noted that it was the right ear. The blow was likely meant for the man's head, but it missed and wounded his ear instead.

Jesus immediately ordered a halt to the violence, telling His followers to put an end to fighting. He reached out, touched the servant's ear, and healed him completely. Even in the middle of being arrested, Jesus showed mercy to His enemies and proved that He was giving Himself up voluntarily.

differ.view: Some take Jesus' words as a polite request to his captors to let his hands go so he could heal the wounded servant.

notes.meaning: Jesus spoke directly to the chief priests, temple officers, and elders who had come out to seize Him. He asked why they came with swords and clubs as if they were tracking down a dangerous bandit or rebel. He had never led a violent revolt, making their weapons completely unnecessary.

Jesus pointed out that He had been teaching openly in the temple courts day after day, yet they had never tried to arrest Him in public. They came at night because this was their allotted time, when evil and the power of Satan were permitted to act. Jesus knew that their temporary triumph was allowed only under God's control.

The armed group seized Jesus and led Him away to the house of the high priest. Peter followed behind the crowd at a distance. He cared enough about his Master not to run away completely, but he lacked the courage to stand openly with Him.

Because it was a chilly spring night, the servants and officers built a fire in the center of the open courtyard and sat down together. Peter walked over and sat among them to warm himself. He tried to blend in with the crowd so nobody would suspect who he was.

A servant girl saw Peter sitting in the firelight and stared closely at his face. Recognizing him in the bright glow, she spoke up and told the crowd that he had been with Jesus. Her sudden statement placed Peter in immediate danger.

Afraid of what might happen to him, Peter denied the charge right away. He told the girl that he did not even know Jesus. In a moment of fear, he broke his earlier promise to stay loyal to his Master.

A short time later, another bystander noticed Peter and insisted that he was one of Jesus' disciples. Peter denied it firmly a second time, telling the man he was mistaken. Each lie pulled Peter deeper into the trap of disowning his Lord.

About an hour later, another man insisted with great confidence that Peter was definitely a follower of Jesus. He pointed out that Peter was from Galilee, since his regional accent gave him away. Peter's attempt to hide his identity was falling apart under closer scrutiny.

Peter denied the charge a third time, claiming he had no idea what the man was talking about. While he was still speaking the words, a rooster crowed in the early morning air. That sound marked the exact sign Jesus had told him to expect.

At the sound of the rooster, the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter. That glance reminded Peter of Jesus' earlier warning that he would deny Him three times before the rooster crowed. The look was full of sorrow and mercy, breaking Peter's heart and waking him to the gravity of his failure.

Crushed by guilt and grief, Peter walked out of the courtyard and cried bitter tears. His weeping came from genuine sorrow over failing the Lord he loved. Unlike Judas, who fell into despair and killed himself, Peter's sorrow led him toward repentance and eventual healing.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Early church teachers saw Peter's bitter weeping as the beginning of penance, showing that believers who fall into serious sin after receiving the Lord's Supper can still be forgiven and restored through penitence.

notes.meaning: The men holding Jesus in custody began to mock Him and beat Him. They insulted Him with cruel words and struck Him while waiting for the full council to gather. In doing so, Jesus bore the shameful mistreatment that the prophets said the Messiah would suffer.

The guards tied a blindfold over Jesus' eyes and struck Him on the face. They sneered and told Him to prophesy by guessing which one of them had hit Him. Because Jesus was known as a prophet, they turned His divine gift into a cruel guessing game.

The men continued to shout many other insulting and slanderous things against Jesus. Luke calls their words blasphemy, which means speaking evil against God. While the council later accused Jesus of blasphemy, Luke shows that the guards were the ones guilty of it by reviling the true Son of God.

At daybreak, the Sanhedrin—the high council of Jewish elders, chief priests, and teachers of the law—assembled for an official meeting. They brought Jesus into their council chamber for a formal trial. They waited until morning because their legal rules required capital trials to be held in daylight.

The council demanded that Jesus state clearly whether He was the Christ, the promised Messiah and King. Jesus answered that even if He told them plainly, they would refuse to believe Him. Their minds were already made up, so they were asking only to find an excuse to condemn Him.

Jesus added that if He asked them questions to prove the truth from Scripture, they would not answer Him or release Him. They had no interest in an honest search for truth. Their sole purpose was to keep Him bound and put Him to death.

Jesus told the council that from then on, the Son of Man would be seated at the right hand of God's mighty power. He was pointing to Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah receiving supreme glory and authority in heaven. This meant that while they were judging Him now, He would one day sit as their ultimate Judge.

Understanding His claim of divine authority, the whole council asked if He was truly the Son of God. Jesus answered, 'You say that I am,' which was a clear way of confirming that their words were correct. He openly claimed to be both the Messiah and God's Son, knowing it would seal His death sentence.

The council members declared that they had no need for more witnesses. They believed they had heard blasphemy straight from Jesus' own lips by His claim to be divine. Based on this confession, they considered His guilt proven and prepared to hand Him over to the Roman governor for execution.
